title: Standard Streams
concept: The standard streams stdin, stdout, and stderr are the default channels for console input and output.

steps.title: Include stdio.h header
steps.explanation:
**`#include <stdio.h>`** — Header for using standard input/output functions.

Every C program automatically receives **three data streams (streams)** from the operating system when it starts.

steps.title: Start main function
steps.explanation:
**`int main() {`** — When the program starts, the OS automatically opens three streams: `stdin`, `stdout`, and `stderr`.

These three are all **`FILE *` type pointers**.

steps.title: Write to standard output (stdout)
steps.explanation: **`fprintf(stdout, "This uses stdout\n");`** — `fprintf` is a function that writes a formatted string to the **specified stream**. The structure is `fprintf(stream, format string, values...)`, and the output destination is specified as the first argument.

steps.title: printf is a shortcut for stdout
steps.explanation: **`printf("printf is a shortcut for fprintf(stdout, ...)\n");`** — The `printf(...)` we've been using is actually a **shortcut** that internally calls `fprintf(stdout, ...)`. i.e. `printf("Hello\n")`
steps.code: printf("printf is a shortcut for fprintf(stdout, ...)\n");

steps.title: Write to standard error (stderr)
steps.explanation: **`fprintf(stderr, "Error: Something went wrong!\n");`** — This time, send the message to **`stderr` (the standard error stream)** instead of `stdout`. By default, `stderr` is also connected to the terminal, so it is indistinguishable from `stdout` at a glance.

steps.title: Variable declaration and input prompt
steps.explanation: **`int n;`** and **`fprintf(stdout, "Enter a number: ");`** — Declare an integer variable `n` to receive user input and print an information message. Since it was declared but not initialized, `n` contains a **garbage value**, and `???` in the visualization indicates this.

steps.title: input simulation
steps.explanation: **`n = 5;`** — We actually read the value from **`stdin`** (standard input attached to the keyboard) with `scanf("%d", &n);`, but this assumes the user typed `5`.

steps.title: Input value confirmation output
steps.explanation: **`fprintf(stdout, "You entered: %d\n", n);`** — Displays the assigned value on the screen through `stdout`. `%d` is replaced with the integer value `5` of `n`, and `"You entered: 5"` is output.

steps.title: Program exit
steps.explanation: **`return 0;`** — When the program terminates normally, the three standard streams are automatically closed, and any data remaining in the `stdout` buffer is also output (flushed).

quiz.question: When you run ./app > log.txt in the terminal, what is displayed on the screen?
quiz.explanation:
The `>` operator sends only stdout to a file.
stderr is still output to the screen (terminal), so you can immediately check the error message.

misconceptions.wrong: You can just use printf, there is no reason to use fprintf.
misconceptions.correct: When learning file input/output, you will need the `fprintf(file, ...)` format, and distinguishing between stdout/stderr is the basis of system programming.
misconceptions.why: Stream separation is essential to follow Unix philosophy (pipelining).

keyTakeaway: stdin, stdout, and stderr are file pointers that are automatically opened when a program starts and communicate with the operating system.
